Contentexpand_moreexpand_lessLearning objectives and content
    ObjectivesWhat are the learning objectives of the course?
After successfully completing this course students will
• be familiar with the abstract definitions of non-cooperative games and strategies,
some specific kinds of games, and how they can be used to model real-world
situations,
• understand the notion of Nash and other types of equilibria and what they mean in
settings modeled by games,
• know how to argue about the existence of equilibria, the complexity deciding their
existence, and the complexity of finding them,
• understand the adaptation of some of the above to cooperative games,
• have gotten a light introduction to mechanism design including classic design
objectives, impossibility results and approaches how to resolve them

    ContentWe plan for the following content:
• An introduction to fundamental game theoretic concepts including the abstract
definition of games, specific games with examples, strategies and equilibria with a
focus on Nash equilibria.
• Algorithmic and complexity theoretic investigation of problems relating to finding
equilibria (Mini-max theorem, Nash’s theorem, Sperner’s lemma, Brower’s fixed point
theorem, a light discussion on the complexity classes PPAD and PLS in this context)
• A light exploration of collaborative games, specifically coalition formation games with
basic concepts stability/rationality concepts studied in this context and a more
detailed analysis of stable matching and the Gale-Shapely algorithm.
• Additionally, we plan on discussing mechanism design theory in the context of one
specific type of games which we will still determine but will be one of
routing/congestion games, tournaments or auctions.
